screens.title: Four trades
screens.prose: Four trades are on offer, each with an expected profit and a number of risk units. The desk's risk limit is 6 units. Choose the trades that give the most profit within the limit. Lesson 2's problem D had this shape with up to 20 instruments.
screens.question: Tap the trades to take.

hints.text: Try every pair that fits the limit.
D is the most profitable. What fits beside it?
D uses 4 units, which leaves 2: B or C. B earns more, so B and D make £11k.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Add up the risk of what you chose, then look for more profit.

byKey.ab: A and B fit, 5 units for £9k. B and D use all 6 units for £11k.
byKey.cd: C and D fit for £10k. B costs the same 2 units as C and earns £1k more.
byKey.abc: A, B and C use 7 units, over the limit of 6.
byKey.d: D alone is £7k and leaves 2 units, enough for B.
byKey.r0: A costs 3 units. Beside D it breaks the limit, and beside B it earns only £9k.
byKey.r2: C earns £1k less than B for the same 2 units.

explain.text: B and D use exactly 6 units for £11k. With four trades there are $2^4 = 16$ subsets, few enough to try every one. Next we name each subset by a number.

screens.title: A subset as a number
screens.prose: Give each item a bit: A is bit 0, B bit 1, C bit 2. A subset is then one number, its **mask**: bit $i$ is 1 when item $i$ is in. Slide through masks 0 to 7.

frames.caption: mask 0 = 000 in binary: the empty set

screens.question: Which mask stands for {A, B}, without C?

hints.text: A is worth $2^0 = 1$ and B is worth $2^1 = 2$.
Find the row with 1s under A and B only.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Add the value of each item's bit.

byKey.reversed: 6 is 110: B and C. You read bit 0 from the left; it is on the right.
byKey.one: 2 is 010, B alone. Add A's bit, worth 1.

explain.text: A is $2^0 = 1$ and B is $2^1 = 2$, so {A, B} is 3, binary 011. Every subset of $n$ items is one number from 0 to $2^n - 1$. Counting from 0 to $2^n - 1$ visits each subset once.

screens.title: Four bit operations
screens.prose: Four operations do most of the work. `mask >> i & 1` reads bit $i$. `mask | 1 << i` adds item $i$. `mask & -mask` keeps the lowest set bit. `bin(mask).count("1")` counts the items. Work them out for mask 10.
screens.question: Fill in each value.

hints.text: Write 10 as 1010 and work bit by bit.
Bit 0 is the rightmost digit.
Bit 1 is 1. Adding bit 2 gives 1110, which is 14. The lowest set bit is 2, and there are two 1s.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Work on the binary 1010.

byKey.r0c1: Bit 1 of 1010 is 1: shift right once to 101, then `& 1` keeps the last bit.
byKey.r1c1: `<<` binds tighter than `|`, so `1 << 2` is 4, and `10 | 4` is 14.
byKey.r2c1: `-10` flips the bits of 10 and adds 1. Only the lowest set bit, worth 2, survives the `&`.

explain.text: These four lines read, add, isolate and count items in a set stored as one integer. Python 3.10 and later also has `int.bit_count()`. In C++ the same operators work on `int`, with `__builtin_popcount` for the count.

screens.title: One shift too few
screens.prose: A loop meant to visit every subset of $n = 4$ items reads `for mask in range(1 << n - 1):`. It runs without an error, and its answer is too small on some tests.
screens.question: How many masks does the loop visit?

hints.text: Which binds tighter in Python, `-` or `<<`?
Arithmetic binds tighter than shifts.
`1 << n - 1` is `1 << 3`, which is 8. Masks 8 to 15 are never visited.

feedback.correct: 8: the loop skips every subset holding item 3.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Bracket the expression the way Python reads it.

byKey.minus-last: 15 is `(1 << n) - 1`. Python reads `1 << n - 1` as `1 << (n - 1)`, because `-` binds tighter than `<<`.
byKey.all: 16 is what was meant. The `- 1` changes the shift instead: `1 << 3` is 8.

explain.text: `1 << n - 1` is $2^{n-1}$, here 8, so every subset containing the last item is skipped. Write `range(1 << n)`, and bracket anything else: `(1 << n) - 1`. In C++ `mask & 1 << i == 0` is a second trap, since `==` binds tighter than `&` there.

screens.title: Count the subsets
screens.prose: Write `count_subsets_with_sum(xs, target)`: how many subsets of `xs` sum to `target`. The empty set counts when `target` is 0. Positions count, so equal values in different places make different subsets. Here $n \le 16$.
screens.question: Write `count_subsets_with_sum(xs, target)`.

widget.solution:
def count_subsets_with_sum(xs, target):
    n = len(xs)
    sums = [0] * (1 << n)
    count = 1 if target == 0 else 0  # the empty set
    for mask in range(1, 1 << n):
        low = mask & -mask
        i = low.bit_length() - 1
        sums[mask] = sums[mask ^ low] + xs[i]
        if sums[mask] == target:
            count += 1
    return count
widget.how: Check runs 10 hidden tests, each expected answer comes from a brute force over `itertools.combinations`. They include repeats, negative values and an empty list. Tests 8 to 10 have $n = 16$.

hints.text: Loop over masks and sum the chosen values.
Mask 0 is the empty set, with sum 0.
For each mask from 0 to $2^n - 1$, add `xs[i]` for each set bit $i$. Count the masks whose sum is `target`.

feedback.correct: Every mask counted once, the empty set included.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Look at the first failing test.

byKey.test-2: Test 2 is the empty list with target 0. The empty subset sums to 0, so the answer is 1.
byKey.test-3: Test 3 is `[5]` with target 0: only the empty set works.
byKey.test-4: Test 4 is `[2, 2, 2]` with target 4: three subsets, one per pair of positions.
byKey.test-5: Test 5 has a negative value: −1 + 2 = 1 counts.

explain.text: A mask loop with an inner sum is $O(2^n n)$. Reusing `sums[mask ^ low]`, the mask without its lowest bit, makes it $O(2^n)$. That is a first **DP over masks**: each mask's answer is built from a smaller mask's.

screens.title: Popcounts by DP
screens.prose: Write `popcounts(n)`: the list of popcounts, the number of 1 bits, of masks 0 to $2^n - 1$. Build each from a smaller mask with `p[m] = p[m >> 1] + (m & 1)`. The last test refuses `bin` and `bit_count`, so the DP does the work.
screens.question: Write `popcounts(n)`.

tests.call: popcounts(3) == [0, 1, 1, 2, 1, 2, 2, 3] and 'bin(' not in __learner_source__ and 'bit_count' not in __learner_source__

widget.how: Check runs 8 hidden tests: $n = 0$ (mask 0 only), 1, 3 and 4. Tests 5 to 7 check the length, sum and last entry for $n = 18$. Test 8 checks `popcounts(3)` and that your code does not call `bin` or `bit_count`.

hints.text: `m >> 1` is $m$ without its last bit, and it is smaller than $m$.
So `p[m >> 1]` is already filled in when you reach `m`.
Start with `p = [0] * (1 << n)`, then for `m` from 1 up set `p[m] = p[m >> 1] + (m & 1)`.

feedback.correct: Each mask from a smaller one, in one pass.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Look at the first failing test.

byKey.test-1: Test 1 has $n = 0$: one mask, 0, with popcount 0, so the list is `[0]`.
byKey.test-8: Test 8 needs `popcounts(3)` right and no `bin` or `bit_count` in your code. Build each entry from `p[m >> 1]` instead.

explain.text: `m >> 1` drops the last bit, giving a smaller mask already filled in. Adding `m & 1` puts that bit back. Filling masks in increasing order is how every DP over masks runs.

screens.title: A tour of 10 cities
screens.prose: The travelling salesman visits $n$ cities once each, starting from city 0, for the least distance. The DP state is a pair: the mask of cities visited, and the city we stand in. Each state tries every unvisited next city.

lines: through exactly mask, ending at j
params.title: Masks and cities

screens.question: For $n = 10$, how many states `(mask, j)` are there?

hints.text: How many masks are there for 10 cities?
$2^{10} = 1{,}024$ masks, and each pairs with an end city.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Multiply the masks by the end cities.

byKey.perms: 362,880 is $9!$, the orders of the other nine cities. The DP merges orders that reach the same set and city.
byKey.masks: 1,024 counts the masks only. Each mask pairs with one of 10 end cities.

explain.text: $10{,}240$ states, each trying up to 10 next cities: about $10^5$ steps, against $9! = 362{,}880$ orders of 10 steps each. The gap widens fast with $n$. At $n = 16$ the DP is $2^{16} \cdot 16^2 \approx 1.7 \cdot 10^7$ steps, already slow in Python.

screens.question: About how many subsets do the two halves list in total?

hints.text: Each half has 20 trades.
One half has $2^{20} \approx 10^6$ subsets.
Two halves: $2 \cdot 2^{20} \approx 2.1 \cdot 10^6$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count the subsets of each half, then add.

byKey.whole: That is $2^{40}$, every subset of all 40. Each half lists only its own $2^{20}$.
byKey.half: That is one half. The other half lists as many again.

explain.text: Two lists of $2^{20}$, about $2 \cdot 10^6$ entries, replace $10^{12}$ masks, and the sort and searches add a log factor. A sum version for $n = 40$ took about 2 s in the app's Python. That is a C++-sized idea at the edge of a Python time limit.

screens.title: When the limit says 2ⁿ
screens.prose:
A small $n$ in the constraints, up to about 20 in C++ and 16 in browser Python, signals masks:

```python
for mask in range(1 << n):        # every subset
    for i in range(n):
        if mask >> i & 1: ...

sub = mask                        # every submask
while sub:
    ...
    sub = (sub - 1) & mask
```
screens.question: Over all masks of $n = 3$ items, how many (mask, submask) pairs are there, counting the empty submask?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. For each item, list where it can be.

byKey.all-pairs: 64 pairs every mask with every mask. A submask may use only bits its mask has.
byKey.masks: 8 counts the masks. Each mask has $2^k$ submasks, where $k$ is its popcount.

explain.text: Each item is outside the mask, in the mask only, or in both: 3 choices, so $3^3 = 27$. Enumerating every submask of every mask is $O(3^n)$, about $4.3 \cdot 10^7$ at $n = 16$. The step `(sub - 1) & mask` jumps straight to the next smaller submask.

screens.title: Choosing signals
screens.prose: A researcher has 6 candidate signals for a combined forecast, as in the `alpha` course's lesson 12. With so few, she backtests every non-empty combination, one mask each.
screens.question: How many backtests is that?

hints.text: Each mask from 0 to $2^6 - 1$ is a combination.
Mask 0 is the empty combination.
$2^6 - 1 = 63$ non-empty masks.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count masks, then drop the empty one.

byKey.empty: 64 includes mask 0, the empty combination, which forecasts nothing.
byKey.perms: 720 is $6!$, the orders of six signals. A combination has no order.
byKey.singles: 6 tests each signal alone, not every combination.

explain.text: $2^6 - 1 = 63$ masks, each naming one combination. With 30 signals that grows to about $10^9$, and a search or a ranking replaces enumeration. Developer interviews ask bit tricks such as `x > 0 and (x & (x - 1)) == 0` for a power of two, and this is where they come from.

ideas: A mask is an integer whose bit $i$ says whether item $i$ is in, so `range(1 << n)` visits every subset.
`mask >> i & 1`, `mask | 1 << i`, `mask & -mask` and a popcount read, add, isolate and count items.
Small $n$ in the constraints signals $2^n$; a DP over masks or meet in the middle stretches it further.

formula.name: Subsets and submasks
formula.note: Every subset is $O(2^n)$; every submask of every mask is $O(3^n)$.

summary.trap: `1 << n - 1` is `1 << (n - 1)` in Python: it skips every subset holding the last item.

quiz.prose: Items A, B, C and D are bits 0 to 3.
quiz.question: Which items does mask 13 hold?

options.why: That reads 1101 from the left as bits 0 to 3. Bit 0 is the rightmost digit.
That is 5, binary 0101: bit 3, D, is missing.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Write 13 in binary and read from the right.

explain.text: $13 = 8 + 4 + 1$, so bits 3, 2 and 0 are set: D, C and A.

quiz.prose: A set of items is stored as `mask`.
quiz.question: What does `mask | 1 << i` give?

options.text: The set with item $i$ flipped in or out
options.why: Flipping is `mask ^ 1 << i`. OR only sets the bit.

options.text: Whether item $i$ is in the set

feedback.correct: OR sets bit $i$, which adds item $i$.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. OR with a single 1 bit sets that bit.

explain.text: `1 << i` has only bit $i$ set, and OR turns that bit on in `mask`. If item $i$ was already in, nothing changes.

quiz.prose: You need every subset of $n$ items, including the empty one and the full one.
quiz.question: Which loop visits them all?

options.why: Python reads that as `1 << (n - 1)`, half the masks.
That stops at $2^n - 2$ and misses the full set.
$n^2$ is not the number of subsets; $2^n$ is.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. The masks run from 0 to $2^n - 1$.

explain.text: `range(1 << n)` stops just before $2^n$, so it ends at $2^n - 1$, the full set. It starts at 0, the empty set.

quiz.question: How many submasks does it have, counting 0 and itself?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Each set bit may be kept or dropped.

byKey.bits: 3 is the number of set bits. Each can be kept or dropped, giving $2^3$.

explain.text: 10110 has three set bits, and a submask keeps any of them. That gives $2^3 = 8$, from 10110 itself down to 0.
